title: Built-in Data Structures and Comprehensions
objectives: Choose between list, tuple, dict and set based on behaviour and time complexity.
Write list, dict and set comprehensions and generator expressions.
Use collections helpers such as Counter, defaultdict and deque.
Explain shallow versus deep copies of nested structures.
Sort complex data with key functions and multiple sort criteria.
definition: Python's built-in data structures are list (ordered, mutable sequence), tuple (ordered, immutable sequence), dict (insertion-ordered mapping of hashable keys to values, backed by a hash table) and set (unordered collection of unique hashable items). Comprehensions are concise expressions that build these collections from an iterable with optional filtering.

theory.heading: Lists and tuples
theory.body: A list is a dynamic array: indexing and append are O(1) (append is amortised), but inserting or deleting at the front is O(n) because elements must shift, and x in list is an O(n) scan. A tuple is an immutable sequence; because it cannot change it is hashable when its items are, so it can be a dict key, and it signals 'fixed record' to readers, for example a (lat, lng) pair or a database row.
points: list.insert(0, x), list.pop(0) and x in list: O(n).
Use collections.deque for O(1) appends and pops at both ends (queues).

theory.heading: Dictionaries and sets
theory.body: dict and set are hash tables. Lookup, insertion and membership tests are O(1) on average, which is why converting a list to a set before many membership checks can turn an O(n*m) algorithm into O(n+m). Keys must be hashable. Since Python 3.7 dicts preserve insertion order as a language guarantee. Sets support mathematical operations: union |, intersection &, difference - and symmetric difference ^.
points: d.get(key, default) avoids KeyError for missing keys.
d.setdefault(key, []).append(v) groups values in one line.
d1 | d2 merges dictionaries (Python 3.9+); {**d1, **d2} works on older versions.
A set removes duplicates but does not keep order; dict.fromkeys(items) dedupes while keeping order.

theory.heading: Comprehensions and generator expressions
theory.body: A comprehension builds a collection in a single readable expression: [f(x) for x in items if cond(x)]. Dict comprehensions use {k: v for ...} and set comprehensions use {x for ...}. Using parentheses instead creates a generator expression, which produces items lazily without building a list in memory, ideal for sum(x * x for x in big_range). Keep comprehensions simple; nested logic belongs in a regular loop.
points: squares = [n * n for n in range(5)]
by_id = {u['id']: u for u in users}
Comprehension variables do not leak into the surrounding scope in Python 3.

theory.heading: The collections module
theory.body: Counter counts hashable items and has most_common(n). defaultdict creates a default value for missing keys, removing if-key-not-in-dict boilerplate. deque is a double-ended queue for BFS and sliding windows. namedtuple and dataclasses give lightweight records with named fields. Knowing these saves time in coding interviews and shows idiomatic Python.
points: deque(maxlen=3) keeps only the last three items.

theory.heading: Copying and sorting
theory.body: Assignment never copies. list(x), x.copy() and x[:] make shallow copies: a new outer container whose items are the same objects, so nested lists are still shared. copy.deepcopy recursively copies nested objects. sorted() returns a new list and list.sort() sorts in place; both are stable and accept key= and reverse=. For multiple criteria return a tuple from the key, for example key=lambda p: (-p.score, p.name) for score descending then name ascending.
points: Shallow copy: new container, shared items.
Sorting is O(n log n) with Timsort and is stable.

example.title: Grouping orders with defaultdict and a comprehension
example.body: Group order amounts by city, then build a summary dict with a comprehension. This is the same shape of work a Django view does after fetching rows, before passing a context to a template.

use_cases.title: Fast lookups
use_cases.description: Index records by id in a dict so a view or API handler can find them in O(1).

use_cases.title: Deduplication
use_cases.description: Sets remove duplicate emails or tags before saving to the database.

use_cases.title: Counting and analytics
use_cases.description: Counter for page views, error codes or most common search terms.

use_cases.title: Queues
use_cases.description: deque for breadth-first search, job queues and recent-history buffers.

demonstration.description: Compare a shallow and a deep copy of a nested list to see which changes are shared.

code.source:
import copy

grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = grid.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(grid)

grid[0].append(99)
print(shallow[0])  # shares inner lists
print(deep[0])     # independent
print({1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 4}, {1, 2} | {5})

takeaways: Lists are dynamic arrays; front insertions and membership tests are O(n).
Dicts and sets are hash tables with average O(1) lookup; keys must be hashable.
Dicts keep insertion order since Python 3.7.
Comprehensions build collections; generator expressions produce items lazily.
Counter, defaultdict and deque remove a lot of boilerplate.
Shallow copies share nested objects; use deepcopy when you need full independence.

interview.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
interview.answer: A list is mutable and a tuple is immutable. Because of that a tuple of hashable items is hashable (usable as a dict key), slightly smaller and faster to create, and communicates a fixed-size record. Lists are for homogeneous collections that grow or change.
interview.explanation: Go beyond 'one is mutable': mention hashability and intent (records versus collections).

interview.question: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?
interview.answer: A set is a hash table: Python hashes the value and jumps to its bucket, giving average O(1). A list must compare items one by one, which is O(n).
interview.explanation: Mention the practical trick of converting a list to a set before repeated membership tests, and that worst-case hash collisions degrade to O(n).

interview.question: Are Python dictionaries ordered?
interview.answer: Yes. Since Python 3.7 insertion order is guaranteed by the language specification (it was an implementation detail of CPython 3.6). Iteration returns keys in the order they were first inserted.
interview.explanation: Interviewers check whether your knowledge is current; mention OrderedDict still exists for move_to_end and order-sensitive equality.

interview.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
interview.answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but references the same inner objects. A deep copy recursively copies all nested objects, so changes to inner lists or dicts are not shared.
interview.explanation: Give the nested list example; this ties into bugs when copying configuration dicts or default data.

interview.question: How would you find the k most frequent words in a text, breaking ties alphabetically?
interview.answer: Normalise the words, count them with collections.Counter (O(n)), then sort the items with key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]) and take the first k. For very large vocabularies heapq.nsmallest(k, items, key=...) avoids sorting everything.
interview.explanation: This combines dicts, sorting with tuple keys and complexity analysis, a common screening question.

practice.title: Top-k word frequency
practice.objective: Use Counter, string normalisation and multi-key sorting to rank words.
practice.statement: Read k on the first line and then any number of lines of text. Split the text on whitespace, strip the punctuation characters . , ! ? ; : ( ) from both ends of each word, convert to lowercase and ignore empty results. Print the number of distinct words, then the k most frequent words with their counts. Sort by count descending, then alphabetically. If there are fewer than k distinct words, print them all. If there are no words, print only 'No words'.
practice.input_format: First line: integer k (k >= 1). Remaining lines: free text (may be empty).
practice.output_format: 'Unique: N' followed by up to k lines 'word count', or 'No words'.

example.input:
3
the cat and the hat. The cat sat!

constraints: Text is ASCII and may span several lines.
Words that become empty after stripping punctuation are ignored.
practice.starter:

lines = sys.stdin.read().splitlines()
k = int(lines[0])
text = ' '.join(lines[1:])

# TODO: normalise words, count them and print the result
practice.solution:
import sys
from collections import Counter

lines = sys.stdin.read().splitlines()
k = int(lines[0])
text = ' '.join(lines[1:])

words = [w.strip('.,!?;:()').lower() for w in text.split()]
counts = Counter(w for w in words if w)

if not counts:
    print('No words')
else:
    print(f'Unique: {len(counts)}')
    ranked = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
    for word, count in ranked[:k]:
        print(word, count)
explanation: Join all text lines so words on different lines are counted together.
Normalise each word with strip and lower in a list comprehension.
Counter counts the non-empty words in one pass.
Sort with a tuple key (-count, word): negative count gives descending frequency, the word breaks ties alphabetically.
Slicing ranked[:k] safely returns fewer items when there are fewer than k words.

quiz.question: What is the average time complexity of checking x in a set?
quiz.explanation: Sets are hash tables, so membership is an average O(1) hash lookup.

quiz.question: What does this comprehension with a condition print?
quiz.code: print([n * n for n in range(6) if n % 2 == 0])
quiz.explanation: range(6) gives 0 to 5; the even numbers 0, 2, 4 are squared.

quiz.question: You need to group a list of (city, user) pairs into a dict of city to list of users with the least code. Which tool fits best?
quiz.explanation: defaultdict(list) creates an empty list for each new key, so you can append directly.

quiz.question: Which key sorts players by score descending and then by name ascending?
quiz.explanation: Negating the numeric score reverses its order while leaving the name ascending; reverse=True would reverse both.

quiz.question: Which of these can be used as a dictionary key?
quiz.explanation: Keys must be hashable; a tuple of immutable items is hashable, while lists, dicts and sets are not.
